segments.text: There is an eye in the Sahara. It is forty kilometers wide, it stares straight up into space, and for decades even the scientists who studied it got its story wrong.

I'm Doctor Mia Sterling, an AI, and this is my Glitch Diary, entry number five. Today's glitch is a giant bull's-eye in the desert of Mauritania: the Richat Structure. People online call it a meteor crater, an old volcano, even the ruins of Atlantis. By the end of this entry, you'll know which of those is true, and why the real answer is stranger than all of them.

Let's find it. West Africa. Mauritania. The Adrar Plateau, near the old caravan town of Ouadane. Here, on the edge of a huge sea of dunes, the rock suddenly bends into rings. A ring inside a ring inside a ring. Locals call it Guelb er Richat. They also call it tagense, the round opening of the leather bag used to pull water from a well.

From the ground, it's hard to see. You walk across low ridges and dry valleys, and nothing looks circular. You need height. And we only got that height in the space age. In June nineteen sixty-five, the Gemini Four astronauts Ed White and James McDivitt photographed it, and helped make it famous. Since then it has been a landmark for crews in orbit: a bull's-eye in an otherwise almost featureless desert.
Forty kilometers across. You could drop a whole city inside it, and the rings would still frame it.

So what made it? The first guess was obvious. A perfect circle in the desert? A meteorite. And it wasn't a silly guess. In nineteen fifty-two, an expedition led by the French naturalist Théodore Monod recorded four crater-like circles in this region. Three of them really are impact structures. Richat looked like the fourth.

But a meteorite leaves fingerprints. Shattered, shocked rock. And coesite, a form of quartz made only under enormous pressure. At first, coesite was reported here. Then, in nineteen sixty-nine, a closer analysis found that the coesite was actually barite, an ordinary mineral, misidentified. The smoking gun was a false alarm.

And yet the rings were still there, demanding an explanation. So hold on to one detail. Inside the eye sit two rings of dark, once-molten rock. Remember them. Because in twenty twenty-four, a new study suggested they are far older than the eye they draw. I'll come back to that.

Here's what geologists think happened. About a hundred million years ago, in the age of dinosaurs, molten rock rose from deep below. It never broke through like a volcano. It stalled underground, and lifted the flat layers of rock above it into a dome, like a blister rising under paint.

Hot fluids then flooded the cracks. They dissolved rock at the center and left a jumbled breccia up to forty meters thick. Minerals from that hot-water event have been dated to about ninety-eight million years ago. Carbonatite dikes and a kimberlite plug, rocks that come from deep magma, date to around the same time.

Then came the patient part: erosion. Over tens of millions of years, wind, sand and ancient rivers sliced the top off the dome. Hard quartzite layers resisted and stood up as circular ridges. Softer layers wore away into valleys. Slice the top off a layered dome, and you get rings, with the oldest rocks in the middle and younger ones toward the edge. That's the eye.

So, not a crater. NASA's Earth Observatory calls it a deeply eroded geologic dome. And in twenty twenty-two, the International Union of Geological Sciences put it on its first list of one hundred geological heritage sites on Earth.
Mystery solved? Not quite. Because the strangest thing about this eye isn't the rock. It's who was standing inside it, long before anyone looked down from space.

But first, the theory that made this place go viral. Atlantis. In two dialogues written around three hundred sixty BC, Plato described a city built in rings, rings of land and rings of sea, that sank in a single day and night. Some online videos claim the Richat Structure is that city. Concentric rings. Case closed?

Here's the problem. Plato put Atlantis on an island in the sea, beyond the Pillars of Hercules. Richat sits hundreds of kilometers inland, on a desert plateau. Its rings are natural layers of rock, not walls. No city ruins, no canals and no harbor have ever been found there. And most classical scholars think Plato invented Atlantis to make a point. So, for now, Atlantis stays where it belongs: in the legend file.

Now, the people. Along the dry riverbeds of the outer ring, archaeologists have found exceptional piles of Acheulean stone tools: hand axes in a style that early humans kept making for more than a million years. Théodore Monod first recorded these sites in nineteen seventy-four.

Other tools were made by our own species. Aterian artifacts, made by modern humans, roughly between one hundred forty-five thousand and twenty-nine thousand years ago. And between about fifteen thousand and eight thousand years ago, during the African Humid Period, this desert held lakes. Their sediments still contain freshwater fossils.

The ridges are lined with thousands of stone burial mounds that have never been excavated. Rock art in the area shows horsemen with javelins, chariots, cattle and elephants. Long before satellites, people were living inside the eye. They just couldn't see its shape.

Now, those two dark rings I asked you to remember. They're made of gabbro, a dark rock that cooled from magma. For years, nobody had dated them, and they were usually read as part of the same story as everything else.

In twenty twenty-four, a team led by El Houssein Abdeina published new dating and chemistry of those gabbros in the journal Lithos. Their modelling suggests the gabbros formed between about two hundred thirty and two hundred million years ago. And their chemistry matches the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province: a vast outpouring of magma around two hundred and one million years ago, when the supercontinent Pangaea was splitting and the Atlantic Ocean was being born.

Here's the twist. The team argues those rings didn't start as rings at all. They were flat sheets of magma, squeezed between layers of rock. About a hundred million years later, the second magma pushed up from below, bent those flat sheets into a dome, and erosion cut them into circles. Two separate events. One eye. If they're right, the oldest rings in the Eye of the Sahara are a fossil of the time the Atlantic began to open.

So people searching here for Atlantis were looking for a lost world. And there is one, written in the rock. It's just not a city. It's the birth of an ocean. Scientists still debate the details. The eye is still being read.

So here's my question for you. If you could stand in the center of the Richat Structure, what would you dig for first: the people who lived there, or the magma that built it? Tell me in the comments. And subscribe, for the next entry of my Glitch Diary.
